status.en: 22 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 100% more than the week before, most of them in La Espriella, Espriella and Catatumbo.
status.nb: 22 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 100 prosent flere enn uken før, flest i La Espriella, Espriella og Catatumbo.

summary.en: President de la Espriella opened a Colombian embassy in Jerusalem, prompting condemnation from Pakistan and other Muslim states, while he also announced a cultural counterrevolution against "wokeism" and ordered the removal of over thirty artworks from the National Museum. Opposition groups protested his budget cuts that threaten the peace tribunal and searches for the disappeared, and the peace tribunal charged former FARC members with anti-Indigenous crimes. An acid-attack survivor cancelled planned euthanasia after a public appeal, and a preacher was killed by a criminal group in Cartagena. 225 battle-related deaths were recorded in 2024, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: President de la Espriella åpnet en colombiansk ambassade i Jerusalem, noe som førte til fordømmelse fra Pakistan og andre muslimske stater, mens han også kunngjorde en kulturell motrevolusjon mot «wokeism» og beordret fjerning av mer enn tretti kunstverk fra Nasjonalmuseet. Opposisjonsgrupper protesterte mot hans budsjettkutt som truer fredsretten og søk etter de forsvunnede, og fredsretten anklaget tidligere FARC-medlemmer for anti-urfolksforbrytelser. En overlevende etter en syreangrep avlyste planlagt eutanasi etter en offentlig appell, og en predikant ble drept av en kriminell gruppe i Cartagena. 225 dødsfall knyttet til kamper ble registrert i 2024, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Colombian conflict
background.extract: The Colombian conflict began on May 27, 1964, and is a low-intensity asymmetric war between the government of Colombia, paramilitary groups, crime syndicates, and far-left guerrilla groups engaged in armed factional hostilities to increase their influence in Colombian territory. Some of the most important international contributors to the Colombian conflict include multinational corporations, the United States, Cuba, and the drug trafficking industry.
